readerTitle: Your demo won one fan. The deal needs five.
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (레스토랑 그룹에 주방 준비량 예측 소프트웨어를 판매) · 인물과 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 여럿이 함께 사는 거래에서는 한 사람을 더 세게 설득하는 것이 아니라, 각자가 묻는 서로 다른 질문에 하나씩 답해야 한다.
misconception: 데모를 본 담당자가 마음에 들어 하면 거래는 거의 끝난 것이다.

sources.text: 컨설팅형 영업과 B2B 구매 위원회의 일반 원리 (특정 연구 수치는 인용하지 않음)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산 확인: 이용료 매장당 월 $200 × 4곳 = 월 $800. 월 음식 폐기 $2,400의 3분의 1 = $800. 따라서 폐기를 약 3분의 1 줄이면 이용료를 감당한다는 문장이 맞습니다.
구매 위원회 평균 인원 같은 외부 통계는 출처 확인이 어려워 일부러 넣지 않았습니다. 추가하려면 1차 출처를 확인하세요.
다음 레슨 예고 문구는 SAL-03 유닛 구성이 확정되면 맞춰 수정하세요.

cards.title: Your demo won one fan. The deal needs five.
body: You sell prep-planning software for restaurants. It uses bookings and past sales to tell kitchens how much to prep each morning, so less food ends up in the bin.
Maya runs operations for a group of four restaurants. After your demo she says, "This is exactly what we need." Many deals stall right after a moment like this. Make four decisions and see why.

image.label: A salesperson and a smiling manager, with four empty chairs behind them
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 레스토랑 사무실에서 노트북 데모를 본 매니저가 활짝 웃고 있음. 뒤쪽에 빈 의자 네 개가 그림자처럼 놓여 있어 '아직 만나지 않은 사람들'을 암시. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Maya is sold. What's your next move?
body: She asks you to "send something over" so she can share it with the team.

options.text: Send a proposal with pricing tonight, while she's excited
options.feedback: You keep the momentum, but the proposal lands with people you've never met, who mostly read the price. It sits unanswered for weeks.

options.text: Ask how decisions like this get made and who else will weigh in
options.feedback: You give up a quick send, but you learn who could block the deal before they do. Maya names four people.

options.text: Offer a free month so she can start right away
options.feedback: Real use can build support, but a trial at one site never reaches the people who approve the spend, or the kitchen that has to use it.

cards.title: The head chef isn't a fan.
body: Say you chose B. Maya lists the owner, who signs; the finance manager; the IT person, who looks after the tablets; and Chef Daniel, who runs all four kitchens.
"Daniel thinks prep software is for big chains," she adds.

options.text: Get the owner's approval first, so Daniel has to go along
options.feedback: It may be faster, but an overruled chef can quietly sink the rollout. Software the kitchen ignores gets cancelled at renewal.

options.text: Ask to visit Daniel's kitchen at prep time and ask what slows his mornings
options.feedback: It costs you an early start, but you hear his real worry instead of guessing at it.

options.text: Send Daniel a video of other chefs praising the software
options.feedback: Proof from peers can help, but it answers a question he didn't ask. You still don't know what worries him.

cards.title: Finance asks: "What does it save us?"
body: Say you chose B. At 7 a.m. Daniel shows you his clipboard. His fear isn't technology. It's an app overriding a prep list it doesn't understand. You show him he can change every number. "If it shrinks the bins at closing, fine."
Now the finance manager wants proof.

image.label: A chef's handwritten prep list next to a tablet showing the same list
image.brief: 새벽 주방의 스테인리스 작업대. 왼쪽에 손글씨 준비 목록이 끼워진 클립보드, 오른쪽에 같은 목록을 보여주는 태블릿. 태블릿 숫자 옆에 연필 아이콘(셰프가 수정 가능)을 강조. 실제 로고 없음.

options.text: Send your standard savings calculator based on industry averages
options.feedback: Quick and tidy, but averages invite the reply "we're not average." Finance trusts its own numbers more than yours.

options.text: Work with Maya to use the group's own waste logs and overtime hours
options.feedback: It takes a week, but the case is built from figures finance already trusts: about $2,400 of food thrown out each month.

options.text: Stress how accurate the forecasting features are
options.feedback: Features describe what the software does, not what the business gets. Finance can't put "accuracy" in a budget.

cards.title: The final meeting. Who does the talking?
body: Say you chose B. At $200 per restaurant, the software costs $800 a month. It pays for itself if waste falls by about a third.
The owner calls everyone together and gives you 30 minutes.

options.feedback: You control the message, but to the room you're still an outsider with a target to hit. Their own people are more convincing.

options.text: Maya presents the case, Daniel speaks for the kitchen, you answer questions
options.feedback: You give up the spotlight. In return the owner hears from her own team that their concerns were handled.

options.text: Skip the meeting and send the slides for them to review
options.feedback: It saves time, but objections come up after you've left, with no one in the room to answer them.

cards.title: A buying committee asks many questions, not one.
body: Say you chose B again. The owner asks only, "What if it doesn't work?" Maya has already agreed a three-month pilot at two sites, with waste tracked weekly. IT had a short call about tablets. The owner signs.
A **buying committee** is the group of people who each judge a purchase from their own seat. Does it fit my kitchen? Does it pay? Will it work on our devices? What if it fails?
Winning meant answering each question, mostly through Maya.

image.label: Five people around a table, each with a different question bubble
image.brief: 원탁에 다섯 명. 각자 머리 위 말풍선: 셰프 "Fits my kitchen?", 재무 "Does it pay?", IT "Works on our tablets?", 오너 "What if it fails?", 운영 매니저 "Can I make the case?". 매니저의 말풍선에서 다른 말풍선들로 점선이 이어짐.

cards.title: Match the effort to the deal.
body: Not every sale has a committee. A single café owner buying a $30 app decides alone. Mapping stakeholders there wastes both your time.
This approach is also slow: weeks of visits instead of one email. It pays off when the purchase is large, shared or risky.
And a champion isn't a puppet. If Maya backed something that didn't fit, she would lose trust with people she works with every day. Build support only for deals that truly help them.

cards.title: In group buying, each person needs their own reason to say yes.
body: Each decision you made maps to an idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1,** asking who else decides: many decision makers
**Decision 2,** visiting the kitchen first: questions before pitches
**Decision 3,** using their own waste logs: building a business case
**Decision 4,** letting Maya present: finding a champion
cards.callout: **Try it today:** pick one open deal or proposal. Write down everyone who will weigh in and the one question each will ask. Circle anyone you haven't spoken to yet.
